data set in M&L, because the Cashflow 101 data set provided by M&L does not contain the
auction titles. Therefore, my primary empirical test does not apply directly to the primary results
in M&L. However, I discuss why wording differences may be important for this product as well.
I also argue that other results in M&L are consistent with search costs. One is that the
overbidding rate is higher among auctions with a larger spatial separation in search results from
the BIN. Search costs could generate this result because a larger separation would make it more
difficult to find both listings. I also apply my test to a new eBay data set of 552 new movie-DVD
auctions. I find significant overbidding here (23 percent of auctions), but a close connection
between wording and overbidding as well.

The purpose of the study was to investigate the development of L2 automaticity at

the sentence level and to validate the use of CV as a measure of L2 automatization

in sentence processing. The study was a partial conceptual replication of Hulstijn

et al. (2009), using the same analyses on a subset of the same speeded tasks.
Compared to Hulstijn et al., however, the current study made important changes to

the data collection and data analysis procedures: (a) participants’ L1 background

was restricted to Korean, which is typologically distinct from English; (b) learners’

English proﬁciency was assessed independently via an online English diagnostic

test; (c) participants were likely more advanced than the high school students

in Hulstijn et al.; and (d) the sentence stimuli in the speeded tasks were made

shorter.
As a result, the CV in the sentence-related tasks did decrease as learners’

proﬁciency level increased, suggesting that the different ESL groups in this study

differed in the automatization of their L2 processing skills. This result was found
decision.reason: Although Lim and Godfroid (2014) evaluate Segalowitz and Segalowitz's (1993) theoretical hypothesis that automatization via cognitive restructuring produces a disproportionate reduction in SD relative to RT (lowering the coefficient of variation, CV, and yielding positive CV-RT correlations) and cite their 1993 word-recognition experiments (including Exp. 2) in discussing longitudinal and cross-sectional designs, they do not re-test Segalowitz and Segalowitz's (1993) empirical word-recognition study (using a word-level semantic classification task only as a baseline control for lexical automaticity). Under Codebook Step 2, a target must be a study whose specific published empirical finding is re-tested, and in a replication chain only the closest study is coded. The paper explicitly states that it is a partial conceptual replication of Hulstijn, Van Gelderen, and Schoonen (2009, Experiment 1; doi:10.1017/S0142716409990014), re-testing sentence-level CV automatization with modified Hulstijn et al. stimuli and their four-step data-cleaning procedure (making row 2418 a duplicate of row 67).

DISCUSSION

Comparison of ﬁndings with Hulstijn et al.’s experiment 1
In this study, we reported the ﬁndings for two sets of statistical analyses that were

conducted before and after cleaning participants’ RTs for three speeded tasks.

The general ﬁnding was that RTs, standard deviations, and CVs all decreased as a

function of participants’ English proﬁciency level: from intermediate ESL learners

(L1 Korean), to advanced ESL learners, to native English speakers. This ﬁnding

was in stark contrast to Hulstijn et al.’s (2009) study, who failed to ﬁnd a decrease
in Dutch high school students’ CV over three consecutive grade years, in which
decision.reason: For the corrected original study Hulstijn, Van Gelderen, and Schoonen (2009, Experiment 1), both studies found decreasing RTs and SDs with proficiency (Table 4), but on the focal sentence-level coefficient of variation (CV) findings Hulstijn et al. (2009) found no CV decrease across Grades 8-10 and questioned CV's validity at the sentence level unless data were cleaned. In contrast, Lim and Godfroid (2014) found that sentence-level CVs decreased as proficiency increased—most robustly both before and after data cleaning in sentence construction (p < .001) and after cleaning in combined sentence verification (p <= .001, though raw verification CV p = .190, plausible-only verification CV did not differ across groups, and cleaned verification coincided with a negative CV-RT correlation r = -.516 in the intermediate group), while noting in the Conclusion (pp. 26-27) that whether smaller CV truly indexes automaticity remains an open, somewhat circular theoretical question. Because the authors explicitly state that their general finding of decreasing CV is 'in stark contrast to Hulstijn et al.'s (2009) study, who failed to find a decrease', the empirical replication outcome for Hulstijn et al. (2009) is 'failed'.
